claim: Intact-organism imaging of Drosophila larvae reveals and quantifies chromatin-aqueous phase separation.
source: Intact-organism imaging of Drosophila larvae reveals and quantifies chromatin-aqueous phase separation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and is supported by experimental data referenced in the manuscript (Amiad-Pavlov et al., 2020).

claim: Chromatin can be organized near the lamina layer of the nuclear envelope.
source: The chromatin can be organized near the lamina layer of the nuclear envelope, conventionally fill the nucleus, be organized centrally, or as a wetting droplet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract and supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Chromatin can conventionally fill the nucleus.
source: The chromatin can be organized near the lamina layer of the nuclear envelope, conventionally fill the nucleus, be organized centrally, or as a wetting droplet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract and supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Chromatin can be organized centrally in the nucleus.
source: The chromatin can be organized near the lamina layer of the nuclear envelope, conventionally fill the nucleus, be organized centrally, or as a wetting droplet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract and supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Chromatin can be organized as a wetting droplet.
source: The chromatin can be organized near the lamina layer of the nuclear envelope, conventionally fill the nucleus, be organized centrally, or as a wetting droplet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract and supported by experimental imaging data.

claim: Chromatin organizational transitions are controlled by changes in nuclear volume.
source: These transitions are controlled by changes in nuclear volume and the interaction of chromatin with the lamina (part of the nuclear envelope) at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations and simulations.

claim: Chromatin organizational transitions are controlled by the interaction of chromatin with the lamina at the nuclear periphery.
source: These transitions are controlled by changes in nuclear volume and the interaction of chromatin with the lamina (part of the nuclear envelope) at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations and simulations.

claim: The competition of chromatin self-attraction and chromatin binding to the lamina determines the mode of chromatin distribution.
source: Using a simple polymeric model that includes the key features of chromatin self-attraction and its binding to the lamina, we demonstrate theoretically that it is the competition of these two effects that determines the mode of chromatin distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The qualitative trends obtained in simulations compare well with observed intact-organism imaging and quantification.
source: The qualitative trends as well as the composition profiles obtained in our simulations compare well with the observed intact-organism imaging and quantification.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through comparison of simulation results with experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin is a complex, linear macromolecule comprising DNA and histone proteins.
source: Chromatin is a complex, linear macromolecule comprising DNA and histone proteins which in eukaryotic cells, is localized in the nucleus where it is solubilized in water, salts, and other small molecules (Cooper and Hausman, 2000; Phillips et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to textbooks.

claim: In eukaryotic cells, chromatin is localized in the nucleus where it is solubilized in water, salts, and other small molecules.
source: Chromatin is a complex, linear macromolecule comprising DNA and histone proteins which in eukaryotic cells, is localized in the nucleus where it is solubilized in water, salts, and other small molecules (Cooper and Hausman, 2000; Phillips et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: In the conventional picture, chromatin and aqueous solvent uniformly fill the nucleus as a single phase.
source: In this 'conventional' picture, the chromatin and the aqueous solvent uniformly fill the nucleus as a single phase (Rosa and Shaw, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the conventional model and supported by citation.

claim: The conventional picture accounts for phase separation similar to that of soluble AB block copolymers, with regions of transcriptionally active euchromatin separated from regions of relatively inactive heterochromatin.
source: Even the conventional picture accounts for phase separation similar to that of soluble AB block copolymers (Rubinstein and Colby, 2003), with regions of transcriptionally active euchromatin (A block) separated from regions of relatively inactive heterochromatin (B block); however, both are assumed to be homogeneously solubilized in the aqueous phase (Erdel and Rippe, 2018; Narlikar, 2020; Strom et al., 2017; Larson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the conventional model and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hi-C experiments reveal AB chromatin compartmentalization.
source: For example, Hi-C experiments reveal such AB chromatin compartmentalization (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009) but do not provide information about their location within the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding and supported by citation.

claim: Hi-C experiments do not provide information about the location of chromatin compartments within the nucleus.
source: For example, Hi-C experiments reveal such AB chromatin compartmentalization (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009) but do not provide information about their location within the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of Hi-C experiments.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy reveals a 'marshland' of chromatin and aqueous phase, with a non-uniform distribution of chromatin at the submicron level.
source: However, recent super-resolution microscopy reveals a 'marshland' of chromatin and aqueous phase, with a non-uniform distribution of chromatin at the submicron level (Cremer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by citation.

claim: A study observed larger scale phase separation of chromatin and the aqueous phase in early development, with chromatin localized to the nuclear periphery.
source: Another study observed a larger scale phase separation of chromatin and the aqueous phase in early development, with the chromatin localized to the nuclear periphery (Popken et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by citation.

claim: Intact-organism imaging of Drosophila larvae nuclei reveals chromatin-aqueous phase separation controlled by changes in nuclear volume and chromatin-lamina interactions.
source: More recently, we have presented (see Appendix 1—figure 1) intact-organism imaging of Drosophila larvae nuclei where the chromatin was labeled by H2B-RFP, and the nuclear envelope was labeled by Nesprin/Klar-GFP. These experiments reveal and quantify chromatin-aqueous phase separation and its control by changes in the nuclear volume and the interaction of chromatin with the lamina (part of the nuclear envelope) at the nuclear periphery (Amiad-Pavlov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding and supported by citation and reference to figure.

claim: The model focuses on the concentration profile of chromatin within the nucleus when chromatin self-attraction and chromatin-lamina interaction are larger than the difference between AA and BB interactions.
source: The model we present below that focuses on the concentration profile of chromatin (whether A or B) within the nucleus, is appropriate when the chromatin self-attraction relative to the chromatin-aqueous phase interaction, as well as the chromatin-lamina interaction are larger than the difference between the AA and BB interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a condition for the applicability of the model.

claim: The nuclear envelope contains lamina which is a dense, fibrillar network of proteins that provide anchoring points for various proteins that bind to chromatin on one end and the lamina on the other.
source: The nuclear envelope contains lamina which is a dense, fibrillar network of proteins that provide anchoring points for various proteins that bind to chromatin on one end and the lamina on the other (Ulianov et al., 2019; Kind et al., 2013; Yáñez-Cuna and van Steensel, 2017; Meister et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lamins comprise two A-type (lamin A and lamin C) and two B-type (lamin B1 and lamin B2) proteins in general.
source: These binding proteins associate with lamins that, in general, comprise two A-type (lamin A and lamin C) and two B-type (lamin B1 and lamin B2) proteins (Moir et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila has only one A-type lamin (lamin C) and one B-type lamin (lamin Dm0) gene.
source: However, Drosophila has only one A-type lamin (lamin C) and one B-type lamin (lamin Dm0) gene (Riemer et al., 1995; Schulze et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: A-type and B-type lamins are found at the nuclear periphery while A-type lamins are also found in the nuclear interior.
source: A-type and B-type lamins are found at the nuclear periphery while A-type lamins are also found in the nuclear interior (Briand and Collas, 2020; Naetar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Chromatin domains that bind to lamins are called lamina associated domains (LADs).
source: Those chromatin domains, which bind to the lamins are called lamina associated domains (LADs) which are similarly divided in two groups: A-LAD and B-LAD corresponding to interactions with A-type lamin and B-type lamin, respectively (van Steensel and Belmont, 2017; Briand and Collas, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: LADs are divided into A-LAD and B-LAD corresponding to interactions with A-type lamin and B-type lamin, respectively.
source: Those chromatin domains, which bind to the lamins are called lamina associated domains (LADs) which are similarly divided in two groups: A-LAD and B-LAD corresponding to interactions with A-type lamin and B-type lamin, respectively (van Steensel and Belmont, 2017; Briand and Collas, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The anchor protein lamin B receptor (LBR) binds lamin B and acts as a tether between chromatin and the nuclear lamina.
source: The anchor protein lamin B receptor (LBR) binds lamin B and acts as a tether between chromatin and the nuclear lamina (Solovei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: Experiments performed in the absence of LBR observed a loss of peripheral LADs and an inverted architecture with LADs localized within the nuclear interior.
source: Experiments performed in the absence of LBR observed a loss of peripheral LADs and an inverted architecture with LADs localized within the nuclear interior (Solovei et al., 2013; Briand and Collas, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by citations.

claim: The role of lamin Dm0 in Drosophila is the same as LBR in mammalian cells.
source: The role of lamin Dm0 in Drosophila is the same as LBR in mammalian cells (Wagner et al., 2004; Ulianov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: If chromatin were a self-avoiding polymer, its radius of gyration in aqueous solution would typically be larger than the diameter of the nucleus.
source: However, if chromatin were a self-avoiding polymer (with no self-attraction), its radius of gyration in aqueous solution would typically be larger than the diameter of the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical consideration based on polymer physics.

claim: Under confinement, a self-avoiding chromatin polymer would fill the entire volume of nucleus, which is not consistent with the observation of peripheral or central chromatin organization.
source: Thus, under confinement, chromatin would fill the entire volume of nucleus, which is not consistent with the observation (Amiad-Pavlov et al., 2020) of peripheral or central chromatin organization.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical inference that is inconsistent with experimental observations.

claim: Experimental observations of peripheral organization demonstrate the condensation of chromatin in the outer part of the nucleus, indicating the presence of chromatin self-attraction.
source: The experimental observations (see Appendix 1—figure 1) of peripheral organization demonstrate the condensation of chromatin in the outer part of the nucleus, indicating the presence of chromatin self-attraction (Amiad-Pavlov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from experimental observations and supported by citation and figure reference.

claim: Positively charged histone tails attract negative DNA linkers and can promote condensation of chromatin.
source: For example, the positively charged histone tails attract negative DNA linkers and can thus promote condensation of chromatin (Gibson et al., 2019; Bajpai and Padinhateeri, 2020; Hancock, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism for chromatin self-attraction and supported by citations.

claim: Protein condensates that interact with chromatin can result in chromatin self-attraction.
source: Protein condensates that interact with chromatin can also result in self-attraction.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism for chromatin self-attraction.

claim: Phase separation of HP1 in the nucleus binds to heterochromatin domains of chromatin.
source: A prominent example is the phase separation of HP1 in the nucleus, which binds to the heterochromatin domains of chromatin (Strom et al., 2017; Larson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an example of protein-chromatin interaction and supported by citations.

claim: If one protein can bridge two or more chromatin regions that are close in physical space, this can result in an effective chromatin-chromatin attraction.
source: If one protein can bridge two or more chromatin regions that are close in physical space, but possibly far along the stretched chromatin chain, this can also result in an effective chromatin-chromatin attraction.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism for chromatin self-attraction.

claim: Nucleoplasmic lamin A can act to 'crosslink' two chromatin regions in vivo.
source: For example, nucleoplasmic lamin A can act to 'crosslink' two chromatin regions in vivo (Bronshtein et al., 2016; Bronshtein et al., 2015; Stephens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an example of chromatin crosslinking and supported by citations.

claim: Chromatin can act as a polymer gel cross-linked by non-histone protein complexes.
source: Other studies have indeed considered chromatin to act as a polymer gel cross-linked by non-histone protein complexes (Biggs et al., 2019; Irianto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a model from other studies and supported by citations.

claim: Changes in nuclear volume have been demonstrated to result in changes in gene expression.
source: This may be why changes in nuclear volume have been demonstrated to result in changes in gene expression (Jain et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by citations.

claim: Comparing live to fixed cells showed a reduction in nuclear volume by a factor of about three and a transition from peripheral (live) to conventional (fixed) chromatin organization.
source: Comparing the live to fixed cells showed a reduction in the nuclear volume by a factor of about three and a transition from peripheral (live) to conventional (fixed) chromatin organization.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from the intact-organism experiments.

claim: Lamin C overexpression resulted in a transition from peripheral (WT) to central (and wetting droplet) organization in the mutant.
source: Lamin C overexpression resulted in a transition from peripheral (WT) to central (and wetting droplet) organization in the mutant (see Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and supported by figure reference.

claim: 48% of the sequences of chromosome X are LAD with an average domain size of 90 kbp.
source: That data indicates that 48% of the sequences are LAD with an average domain size of 90 kbp.
evidence: This is stated as data from an online source.

claim: A decrease in the value of ψ results in a transition of the chromatin organization from peripheral to central.
source: The left hand panel of Figure 3, shows that a decrease in the value of ψ results in a transition of the chromatin organization from peripheral to central.
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result and shown in Figure 3.

claim: As the volume fraction of chromatin decreases, the organization shows a transition from conventional to peripheral.
source: As we decrease the volume fraction of chromatin, the organization shows a transition from conventional to one that is more peripheral.
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result.

claim: In peripheral organization, euchromatin and heterochromatin regions do not separate in the radial directions, but are separated in the perpendicular (angular) direction.
source: An interesting experimental feature observed in the peripheral organization of chromatin, is that euchromatin (active chromatin, typically associated with non-LAD) and heterochromatin (inactive chromatin, typically associated with LAD) regions do not separate in the radial directions, but are separated in the perpendicular (angular) direction (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Angular separation of LAD and non-LAD can occur even if the self-attraction of LAD and non-LAD are the same.
source: Our simulations show that this can be the case even if the self-attraction of LAD and non-LAD are the same; this corresponds to the limit of negligibly small differences in heterochromatin/euchromatin interactions relative to their interactions with the aqueous phase and with the lamina.
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result.

claim: The angular separation of LAD and non-LAD originates in the stronger binding of the LAD domains to the lamina.
source: In this case, the angular separation originates in the stronger binding of the LAD domains to the lamina.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the simulation result.

claim: Lamin overexpression has been suggested to repress the bonding activity of LBR proteins that bind the LAD domains to lamin B.
source: Lamin overexpression has been suggested to repress the bonding activity of LBR proteins that bind the LAD domains to lamin B (Buxboim et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a suggested mechanism and supported by citations.

claim: The model treats a single chromosome.
source: For the understanding of the generic properties of interest here, we treated a single chromosome.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model.

claim: Aqueous phase separation in case of multiple chromosomes can be mapped from the single chromosome results by using the appropriate chromatin volume fraction.
source: Aqueous phase separation in case of multiple chromosomes can be mapped from our results by using the appropriate chromatin volume fraction.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about how the model can be extended.

claim: 48% of the sequences of chromosome X are LAD.
source: In order to simulate a specific system, we modeled the 22.4 Mbp regions of chromosome X (ChrX) of Drosophila where the distribution of the LAD regions is available online (Ho et al., 2014). That data indicates that 48% of the sequences are LAD with an average domain size of 90 kbp.
evidence: This is stated as data from an online source and supported by citation.

claim: The data shows an alternating pattern of LAD and non-LAD along the chromosome length.
source: We analyzed the data which shows an alternating pattern of LAD and non-LAD along the chromosome length (see Appendix 3—figure 1) and used these patterns in our simulations.
evidence: This is stated as a result of data analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: The coarse-grain model does not depend on the size of the chromosome and the locations of the LADs along the chromosome.
source: To demonstrate that our coarse-grain model does not depend on the size of the chromosome and the locations of the LADs along the chromosome, we also used a Monte-Carlo method to randomly distribute the LAD regions along the chain (see details of method and results in Appendix 4, Appendix 4—figures 1, and Appendix 4—figures 2).
evidence: This is stated as a demonstration from additional simulations shown in appendix figures.

claim: The LAMMPS package is used for the Brownian dynamics simulations.
source: The LAMMPS package is used for our calculations (Plimpton, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the simulation method and supported by citation.

claim: The chromosome has a persistence length of 2 beads (1.2 kb) based on a previous estimate of 1–2 kb for interphase chromatin.
source: The chromosome has a persistence length of 2 beads (1.2 kb) which is based on a previous estimate (Marko and Siggia, 1997) of a persistence length of 1–2 kb for interphase chromatin.
evidence: This is stated as a model parameter based on a previous estimate and supported by citation.

claim: Lamins prevent chromosomes from mixing and help chromosomes remain in well-defined regions (analogous to territories).
source: We have also shown that lamins prevent chromosomes from mixing and help chromosomes remain in well-defined regions (analogous to territories) (see Appendix 6—figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result and shown in appendix figure.

claim: Like conventional organization, peripheral chromatin is also organized in a fractal manner.
source: We have also shown that like conventional, peripheral chromatin is also organized in a fractal manner (see Appendix 6—figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result and shown in appendix figure.

claim: Chromatin in peripheral organization is condensed in a manner similar to conventional organization but is more condensed compared with central organization.
source: The results show that chromatin in peripheral organization is condensed in a manner similar to conventional organization but is more condensed compared with central (Appendix 6—figure 1a and (b)) organization.
evidence: This is stated as a simulation result and shown in appendix figure.
